article.title: Why a Good Metric Can Become a Bad Target

paragraphs.en:
Metrics are essential because organizations cannot manage every goal through intuition alone. A sales team needs measures of pipeline health, a product team needs measures of engagement, and a service organization needs measures of quality. Yet a useful metric can become misleading once people are strongly rewarded for maximizing it. This tension is often summarized by Goodhart’s law: when a measure becomes a target, it can cease to be a good measure.

The problem is not measurement itself. The problem is that most metrics are proxies for broader goals. Call-handling time, for example, may be used as a proxy for operational efficiency. If managers simply observe it, the metric can reveal bottlenecks. But if employees are punished whenever calls exceed a strict threshold, they may rush customers, transfer difficult cases, or end conversations before problems are solved. The number improves while the underlying service deteriorates.

The same pattern appears in sales. Suppose a company rewards representatives for the number of qualified opportunities created. If the qualification rule is weak, representatives may label marginal leads as qualified. Pipeline volume rises, but conversion falls and forecasting becomes less reliable. People are not necessarily behaving irrationally; they are responding to the incentive system they were given.

Data and AI teams face similar risks. If a model is judged only by click-through rate, it may learn to promote sensational content that generates clicks but harms long-term satisfaction. If an analyst is rewarded for the number of experiments launched, teams may run many low-value tests rather than a smaller number of decision-relevant experiments. A proxy captures one dimension of value and leaves others exposed.

This is why KPI design should begin with a causal story about the outcome the organization actually wants. What behavior is the metric supposed to represent? Under what conditions could the metric move without the real outcome improving? Who can influence the number, and what shortcuts become attractive when rewards depend on it? These questions turn metric design into governance rather than arithmetic.

One defense is to use a metric portfolio. A primary KPI can be paired with guardrails. A customer-support team might track resolution rate and customer satisfaction alongside handling time. A growth team might monitor conversion together with cancellation, complaint, or retention measures. Guardrails make it harder to improve one number by quietly damaging another important outcome.

Another defense is to separate diagnostic metrics from incentive metrics. A detailed operational measure can be extremely useful for learning without being suitable for compensation. Once money, promotion, or public ranking depends on a number, the organization should assume behavior around that number will change. The measurement system itself becomes part of the system being measured.

Targets also need context. A fixed target can become unreasonable when market conditions, customer mix, or strategy changes. Teams may then spend energy negotiating definitions or shifting activity across reporting periods. Periodic review of definitions, data quality, and unintended behavior is therefore part of KPI maintenance.

Goodhart-type failures can also arise without deliberate gaming. A proxy may work well in the historical environment but break when the product, population, or process changes. Optimizing the proxy pushes the organization into regions where the old relationship between metric and outcome no longer holds. This is one reason strong optimization requires stronger validation.

None of this means targets are useless. Clear goals can focus attention and coordinate action. The lesson is that a metric is an imperfect representation of reality. Strong incentives magnify the consequences of its imperfections.

A mature organization asks two questions at the same time: ‘Is the metric improving?’ and ‘Is the outcome we actually care about improving for the reasons we intended?’ When those answers diverge, leaders should investigate the incentive and measurement design rather than celebrate the dashboard. Good KPI governance preserves the informational value of metrics while reducing the temptation to optimize the score instead of the goal.
paragraphs.zh:
指標是管理不可或缺的工具，但當指標直接變成強力考核目標時，它可能失去原本代表真實目標的能力。Goodhart’s law 常被概括為：當 measure 成為 target，它就可能不再是好的 measure。根本問題在於 KPI 通常只是 broader goal 的 proxy。

例如客服若只被要求縮短 handling time，員工可能加快掛電話或轉移難題，數字改善但服務品質下降；業務若只獎勵 qualified opportunities 數量，可能放寬 qualification，pipeline 變大但 conversion 惡化；AI 若只最佳化 CTR，也可能犧牲長期滿意度。這些行為往往是 incentive system 的合理反應。

因此 KPI design 應從真正想改善的 outcome 與 causal story 出發，搭配 guardrail metrics，並區分 diagnostic metrics 與 incentive metrics。當金錢、升遷、排名和數字綁定時，measurement system 本身就會改變被測量的行為。

Goodhart failure 也不一定來自故意 gaming；環境或客群改變後，原本 proxy 與 outcome 的關係可能失效。成熟的治理應同時問：「指標有沒有改善？」以及「真正重視的結果是否以預期機制改善？」若兩者分離，就應檢查 incentive 與 measurement design，而不是只慶祝 dashboard。
paragraphs.ja:
指標は組織運営に不可欠ですが、強い評価目標にすると本来の目的を表さなくなることがあります。Goodhart’s lawは「measureがtargetになると、良いmeasureでなくなることがある」という問題を示します。多くのKPIは真の目的そのものではなくproxyだからです。

例えば応対時間だけを厳しく評価すると、担当者は難しい問い合わせを転送したり早く通話を終えたりして、数値を改善しながらサービス品質を悪化させる可能性があります。営業の案件数、AIのCTR、実験本数などでも同じです。人は必ずしも不合理なのではなく、与えられたincentiveに適応しています。

そのためKPI設計では、何を本当に改善したいか、その指標がどの行動をproxyしているか、どんな抜け道があるかを考えます。primary KPIにguardrailを組み合わせ、診断用指標と報酬用指標を分けることも有効です。

さらにgamingがなくても、環境や顧客構成が変わればproxyとoutcomeの関係は崩れます。「指標が改善したか」と「本当に望む結果が意図した理由で改善したか」を同時に確認することが、KPI governanceの核心です。

vocabulary.usage: The KPI is only a proxy for the real goal.
Service can deteriorate while the metric improves.
Marginal leads may be labeled qualified.
Pair the primary KPI with guardrails.
Metric design is a governance problem.
Not every diagnostic metric should drive compensation.
The metric and real outcome may diverge.

business.term: What behavior will this target incentivize?
business.explanation: 設計 KPI 時先思考目標會誘發什麼行為。

business.term: We need guardrails around the primary KPI.
business.explanation: 避免單一 KPI 被最佳化時傷害其他重要 outcome。

business.term: The metric improved, but did the underlying outcome improve?
business.explanation: 區分 dashboard 數字與真正 business outcome。
